A Need For Conceptual Science Chemistry Is Hard And Math Is Hard But Physics Is In A Different Category

Aug 5, 2016 • Janice Cotcher

“Advanced Theoretical Physics” by mcolly  is licensed under CC BY 2.0

Very few students take traditional physics courses. The pace of material is prohibitive for most students due to the constantly of adding to the curriculum. “[W]e add to the curriculum as the 20th century gives way to the 21st, and we cannot take away the 17th century.” [4] The students who do take the course are required to do enough problems to infer general strategies and then employ them on the test. This is not meaningful learning at all - students are unlikely to face this kind problem-solving in the future and it sets up most students for failure. The average student regards the study of physics as an incomprehensible discipline to all but the brightest students with a scientificc bent. In reality, a physics course should be within the capabilities of the average student. In the words of Paul G. Hewitt, author of Conceptual Physics, “(t)o the nonscience student, physics is enormously interesting… but when paired with problem solving, the price of admission is too high for too many.” [3]

Instead of questioning the pedagogy, physics educators often wonder “Why can’t they do the math?” The failure of transferring the skills learned should not be faulted entirely to mathematics education. Science educators need a more of a say in mathematics curriculum. Perhaps the key to mathematics education is placing it within the context of science courses at all points from elementary through to high school. [4]

For the typical student, “mathematics is a foreign language”. [1] Mathematics is a language used to express physical phenomena elegantly. Instead of urging students to brush up on their mathematical backgrounds, teachers need to depart from the beauty and elegance of mathematical language and speak to students in their own language. “It may be difficult to teach good physics without relying on mathematics, but it does not follow that it is difficult for students to learn good physics without mathematics.” [1] Famed Physics educator, Paul G. Hewitt, pioneered Concepts Before Computation, a three step learning sequence

  • Exploration - Ignite interest with meaningful examples and hands-on activities.
  • Concept Development - Expand understanding with engaging narrative and visuals, multimedia presentations, and a wide range of concept-development questions and exercises.
  • Application - Reinforce and apply key concepts with hands-on laboratory work, critical thinking, and problem solving. [3]

Physics courses usually emphasize the final stage of the learning cycle: application. Skipping over the stages exploration of concept development results in mathematical problem solving being applied to physics before concepts have been digested. From the beginning, students practice manipulating terms in equations they do not understand conceptually. Students gauge success by their ability to match the answers found in the back of their textbooks.

Physics is distinguished from other academic disciplines by its mathematical structure. To physicists, this structure is beautiful. . .But when this structure is applied prematurely to algebraic word problems, before concepts are developed, its beauty and elegance are lost to all but the very few who are attuned to it [2].

Citations [1] P.G. Hewitt. Conceptual Physics-Turning Nonscience Students on to Their Everyday Environments. The Physics Teacher, 10(9):515-522, 1972.

[2] P.G. Hewitt. Conceptually Speaking… Science Teacher, 57(5):54-57, 1990.

[3] P.G. Hewitt and Addison-Wesley Publishing Company. Conceptual physics. Addison-Wesley, 2002.

[4] M. Sobel. Physics for the non-scientist: A middle way. The Physics Teacher, 47:346, 2009.
